summary.text: Al-Andalus refers to the Muslim-ruled territories on the Iberian Peninsula that existed between 711 and 1492.
At its height it covered the entirety of Spain and Portugal, as well as parts of southern France.
Córdoba became a leading cultural and economic centre, and al-Andalus became a conduit for cultural and scientific exchange between the Islamic and Christian worlds.

facts.label: Last Muslim state
facts.value: The Emirate of Granada, which surrendered in 1492

items.prompt: A Muslim army under Tariq ibn-Ziyad lands at Gibraltar in 711. What reason was stated for the landing?

options.label: To answer a revolt that had broken out in North Africa
To win back Septimania in southern France
To step into a civil war among the Visigoths
To help the Franks against Charles Martel

items.explain: The army landed ostensibly to intervene in a Visigothic civil war, then won a decisive victory over King Roderic and brought most of the Visigothic Kingdom under Muslim rule.

items.prompt: A scholar in a northern Christian kingdom learns about new work in trigonometry and surgery from the south. What role did al-Andalus play here?

options.label: It was a conduit for exchange between the Islamic and Christian worlds
It was a closed society that kept knowledge to itself
It was a Christian state that copied Islamic work
It was a trading post with no scholars of its own

items.explain: Achievements that advanced Islamic and Western science came from al-Andalus, and it became a conduit for cultural and scientific exchange between the Islamic and Christian worlds.

items.prompt: When the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba fell, what became of al-Andalus?

options.label: It was absorbed whole by the Christian kingdoms of the north
It was reunited under a new single caliphate in Toledo
It became a province of the caliph in Damascus
It split into taifa states and principalities

items.explain: After the fall of the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba, al-Andalus fragmented into taifa states and principalities, some of which, like Toledo, Zaragoza and Seville, reached considerable territorial extent.

items.prompt: Christian forces capture Toledo, and the small Muslim states fear more attacks. Who steps in to defend the region?

options.label: The caliph in Damascus
The Almoravid empire
The Emirate of Granada
The Kingdom of Asturias

items.explain: After the Christian capture of Toledo in 1085 the Almoravid empire intervened and repelled attacks, then brought al-Andalus under direct Almoravid rule.

items.prompt: Most of the south has fallen to Christian conquest. What is left of Muslim rule in Iberia?

options.label: A single caliphate ruling from Córdoba
A province of the Almohad empire
The Emirate of Granada, a tributary of Castile
Nothing, as all the Muslim states had vanished

items.explain: The Emirate of Granada remained as the last Muslim state on the peninsula. It became a tributary state of the Crown of Castile before surrendering in 1492.

items.prompt: Which origin has the name al-Andalus traditionally been traced to?

options.label: The Visigoths
The Vandals
The Berbers
Atlantis

items.explain: The name has traditionally been derived from the Vandals. Since the 1980s other ideas, such as Atlantis and a Gothic term, have challenged this tradition.

paragraphs.heading: A shifting Muslim realm
paragraphs.text: Al-Andalus is the name for the lands on the Iberian Peninsula that Muslim states ruled at various times between 711 and 1492. It was never one fixed state: different Muslim governments held these lands in different periods. At its widest, under Umayyad rule, it took in most of the peninsula plus Septimania, a region in southern France. Its borders then moved again and again through a long series of conquests that Western historians have traditionally called the Reconquista, until all that was left was the Emirate of Granada in the south.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: The name first appears on coins struck in 716 by the new Muslim government of Iberia. These coins, called dinars, carried writing in both Latin and Arabic. For a long time the name was traced to the Vandals (vándalos in Spanish). Since the 1980s, rival ideas have appeared: Joaquín Vallvé suggested in 1986 that it was a garbled form of Atlantis, Heinz Halm in 1989 linked it to a Gothic word for allotted land, and Georg Bossong in 2002 looked to a layer of language older than the Romans.

paragraphs.heading: The conquest of 711
paragraphs.text: In 711, the commander Tariq ibn Ziyad, serving the Umayyad caliph al-Walid I, landed at Gibraltar with 7,000 soldiers, on the stated grounds of stepping into a Visigothic civil war. He defeated King Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete that July. With the governor Musa ibn Nusayr, he then spent seven years putting most of the Visigothic Kingdom under Muslim control. Tariq's small army was mostly Berbers, while Musa led a mainly Arab force of more than 12,000. Most of the peninsula joined the growing Umayyad Empire under the name al-Andalus, with its regional capital at Córdoba.

paragraphs.heading: Córdoba and the sciences
paragraphs.text: Under the Caliphate of Córdoba, the city grew into one of the leading centres of culture and trade in the Mediterranean, in Europe and in the Islamic world. Scholars in al-Andalus pushed many fields forward: Jabir ibn Aflah in trigonometry, al-Zarqali in astronomy, al-Zahrawi in surgery, Ibn Zuhr in the study of medicines, and Ibn Bassal and Abu'l-Khayr al-Ishbili in farming science. Their work advanced both Islamic and Western science. Al-Andalus also served as a channel through which culture and science passed between the Islamic and Christian worlds.

paragraphs.heading: Breaking apart
paragraphs.text: For much of its history al-Andalus was in conflict with the Christian kingdoms to its north. When the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba fell by 1031, the land split into a patchwork of states called taifas, and some of them, such as Toledo, Zaragoza, Seville and Badajoz, grew quite large. After Christian forces took Toledo in 1085, the Almoravid empire stepped in, pushed back the attacks, and then ruled al-Andalus directly. For the next century and a half it was a province first of the Almoravids and then of their successors, the Almohads, both ruling from Marrakesh.

paragraphs.heading: The last stand at Granada
paragraphs.text: In the end, the Christian kingdoms of the north overpowered the Muslim states of the south. In the 13th century most of the south fell quickly, as Portuguese, Castilian and Aragonese conquests took Gharb al-Andalus, the valley of the Guadalquivir and Eastern al-Andalus. That left the Emirate of Granada as the only Muslim state on the peninsula. It paid tribute to the Crown of Castile and finally surrendered to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492, ending the span of Muslim rule that had begun in 711.
